questions.question: When installing a light fixture in a corrosive area, what type of enclosure would you use?
questions.answer: Type 3X (the 'X' suffix denotes added corrosion resistance)
solution_steps: Enclosure 'Type' selection is governed by the conditions of use and Table 65 (enclosure selection table in Section 2).
The 'X' suffix on a CSA/NEMA enclosure type designates additional corrosion resistance.
Of the options, Type 3X is the only corrosion-rated enclosure.

questions.question: What is the minimum working space required around a 120/240 V single-phase panelboard?
questions.answer: 1.0 meter (3.3 feet) of working space in front of equipment likely to require examination/adjustment while energized
solution_steps: Rule 2-308 1) requires a minimum working space of 1 m with secure footing about electrical equipment containing renewable parts/disconnecting/operating means or requiring examination, adjustment, operation, or maintenance.
A 120/240 V panelboard takes the general 1 m working space.

questions.question: What is the minimum distance required between an outdoor receptacle and a natural gas meter?
solution_steps: Clearances of electrical equipment from gas pressure-relief/metering devices are addressed by Rule 2-328 with the numeric values in Appendix B (NOT Rule 2-320, which is 'Illumination of equipment').
The keyed answer treats a receptacle as non-arcing equipment requiring a minimum 1.0 m clearance from the gas meter.

questions.question: In a dwelling unit, what is the maximum circuit nominal voltage to ground permitted?
solution_steps: Rule 2-110 (Circuit voltage-to-ground — Dwelling units) states branch circuits in dwelling units shall not have a voltage exceeding 150 volts-to-ground.
A 120/240 V single-phase system has 120 V to ground, which complies. (Note: the dwelling 150 V rule is Rule 2-110, not 2-130; Rule 2-130 is flame-spread requirements.)

questions.question: Is it permissible to use a three-way switch to disconnect electrical equipment?
options: B) Yes, but only for specific equipment
C) No, it is not permissible
D) Yes, if it is a double-pole switch
questions.answer: No, it is not permissible. A three-way (3-way) switch has no fixed/marked open (OFF) position, so it cannot positively indicate the disconnected state required of a disconnecting means.
references: Rule 14-500 series (disconnecting means — indication of open position)
solution_steps: A disconnecting means must clearly and positively indicate the open (OFF) position.
A three-way switch has no fixed ON/OFF marking (its position depends on the companion switch), so it cannot serve as a disconnecting means.

questions.question: What is the minimum clearance required between the wall and metal-enclosed equipment, operating at approximately 14.4/8.3 kV, installed in an electrical room? (OCR gave '14.89/8.6 kV')
solution_steps: Working space around equipment with exposed/dead-front high-voltage parts is set by Rule 2-308 4) using Table 56 (which is keyed to voltage and to the type of facing surface, e.g. a wall).
For metal-enclosed equipment at this voltage class against a wall the keyed value is 0.9 m. (Table 56 not in the verified excerpt — exact value flagged for confirmation against Table 56.)

questions.question: What is the minimum headroom of working space required around switchboards or motor control centers where bare live parts are exposed?
questions.answer: 2.2 meters (the CEC requires a minimum headroom of 2.2 m in working space about exposed live parts of switchboards/MCCs)
solution_steps: Rule 2-308 5) requires the minimum headroom of working spaces around switchboards or motor control centres where bare live parts are exposed to be 2.2 m.
Note option D is mislabeled '(8 feet)' in the source; 2.2 m is approximately 7.2 feet.

questions.question: What type of enclosure is suitable for an installation in an area where the electrical equipment is in direct contact with corrosive material and splash of water?
solution_steps: Type 4 provides protection against splashing/hose-directed water; the 'X' suffix adds corrosion resistance.
Corrosive material + water splash → Type 4X (per Table 65 enclosure selection).

questions.question: What is the flame rating requirement of a cable suitable for installation in buildings of combustible construction only?
solution_steps: Flame-spread requirements for insulated conductors/cables in buildings are set by Rule 2-130 (referring to the NBC), with FT flame-test ratings explained in Appendix B. (Note: Rule 2-126 is 'Use of thermal insulation', not flame rating.)
FT1 is the basic vertical-flame rating acceptable for cables in combustible construction; higher ratings (FT4/FT6) are required for non-combustible construction, plenums, and risers.

questions.question: What is the minimum working space required for the switchboard with exposed live parts that is used to supply a 4 kV, 3-phase, 4-wire system?
questions.answer: 1.2 meters (working space in front of exposed live parts at this high-voltage class, from Table 56)
solution_steps: 4 kV is above 750 V; working space for switchboards with exposed live parts is set by Rule 2-308 4) using Table 56 (which is keyed to voltage and facing-surface condition).
The keyed value for this voltage class in front is 1.2 m. (Table 56 not in the verified excerpt — exact value flagged for confirmation against Table 56.)

questions.question: What does "D.P." marking stand for as indicated on a motor nameplate?
solution_steps: 'D.P.' on a motor nameplate/enclosure rating means Drip Proof (the enclosure resists liquids/solids falling at up to 15° from vertical). This is a general motor-marking fact, not a numbered CEC rule.

questions.question: What is the minimum distance permitted between arc-producing electrical equipment and a natural gas meter when installed outdoors?
questions.answer: 1.5 meters (arc-producing equipment must be kept farther from a gas meter than non-arcing equipment)
solution_steps: Clearances of electrical equipment from gas metering/relief devices are addressed by Rule 2-328 with values in Appendix B (NOT Rule 2-320, which is 'Illumination of equipment').
The keyed answer keeps arc-producing equipment farther than non-arcing: 1.5 m vs 1.0 m. (Exact distances are Appendix B values — flagged for confirmation.)

questions.question: What type of enclosure will be required to protect electrical equipment installed in a location where it is exposed to rain, snow and external formation of ice?
questions.answer: Type 3 (outdoor use; protects against rain, snow, and external ice formation)
solution_steps: Type 3 enclosures are rated for outdoor use, providing protection against windblown dust, rain, sleet, and external ice formation (Table 65).
Type 1 is indoor general purpose; Type 5 is for dust (indoor).

questions.question: What is the minimum working space required in front of a panelboard with exposed live bus operating at a voltage of approximately 8.3/14.4 kV? (OCR gave '8.4/14.55 kV')
questions.answer: 1.5 meters (front working space for exposed live parts at this high-voltage class, from Table 56)
solution_steps: At ~14.4 kV the equipment is well above 750 V; working space for exposed live parts is set by Rule 2-308 4) via Table 56.
The keyed front value for this upper high-voltage class is 1.5 m. (Table 56 not in the verified excerpt — exact value flagged for confirmation against Table 56.)

questions.question: What is the maximum voltage to ground for branch circuits in a dwelling unit if the calculated load of the building will not exceed 250 kVA?
solution_steps: Rule 2-110 limits dwelling-unit branch circuits to 150 V-to-ground.

The higher-voltage exception (up to 600Y/347 V) only applies where the calculated load EXCEEDS 250 kV*A and qualified maintenance personnel are available. Since this load does not exceed 250 kVA, the 150 V limit stands. (Dwelling rule is 2-110, not 2-130.)

questions.question: What is the minimum working space around electrical equipment?
questions.answer: 1.0 meter (3.3 feet) of working space in front of equipment that may require examination or adjustment while energized
solution_steps: Rule 2-308 1) sets the general minimum working space about electrical equipment at 1 m with secure footing.

questions.question: Which type of enclosure for electrical equipment should be used where the enclosure is in a carwash with splashing water?
questions.answer: Type 4 (watertight; protects against splashing and hose-directed water)
solution_steps: Type 4 enclosures are watertight and resist splashing and hose-directed water — suitable for a carwash (Table 65).
Type 3R only resists falling rain; Type 5 is for dust. (If corrosive shampoo were also present, Type 4X would be required.)

questions.question: Which type of fusible disconnect enclosure is used on a rooftop (outdoor, exposed to rain) location?
solution_steps: A rooftop fusible disconnect is outdoors and must resist falling rain/snow.
Type 3R is the rainproof outdoor enclosure commonly used for this application (Table 65).
